title: Nammāzhwār and Madhurakavi Āzhwār
body:
Nammāzhwār was born to Kāriyār and Uḍaiyanangaiyār, of the Vellāḷar community, at Tirukkurugūr near Tirunelvēli in the Pāṇḍya land. He was born on the forty-third day of the Kali Yuga, a Friday, under the Viśākha nakshatram, on Śukla Chaturdaśi, in the Kaṭaka lagnam, in the month of Vṛshabha, in Vasanta ṛtu, in the year Pramādi.

The child was extraordinary. For many days he lived in perfect health with his eyes closed, taking no food at all, neither his mother's milk nor anything else. For days together he made no sound. Distressed, his parents laid the child at the shrine of Ādinātha, the Lord of Kurugūr, surrendering to Him the whole burden of the child's upbringing.

Because the child was so unlike other children, he was named Māran. He was also called Saṭhagōpan, for, unlike other infants, he did not allow worldly ignorance to envelop him.

For sixteen long years, Māran sat motionless beneath the tamarind tree in the Ādinātha temple, without food or drink, his eyes closed, seated in padmāsanam, in utter silence. He was a sun in human form, with a radiance that embraced the universe. He is believed to be an avatāram of Vishvaksēna, the commander of the hosts of Sriman Nārāyaṇa in Vaikuṇṭham.

Madhurakavi Āzhwār

At that time an elderly brāhmaṇa scholar named Madhurakavi was on pilgrimage to the shrines of the north. At Ayōdhyā he saw an extraordinary, gentle light glowing like a star in the southern sky. Eager to discover its source, he travelled south. Even when he reached Srirangam, the light still shone further south. He continued his search until he came to Tirukkurugūr, where the light merged into Nammāzhwār, seated in bliss beneath the tamarind tree.

The First Words

With great difficulty, Madhurakavi succeeded in drawing Nammāzhwār out of his deep samādhi. He became his disciple and learned from him the secrets of all the Śāstras. From then on he remained at his lotus feet, recording the divine poetry that welled up from Nammāzhwār's heart in the ecstasy of Kṛshṇa bhakti, sometimes in a rapid stream and sometimes slowly, according to the intensity of the Āzhwār's inspiration. At the very thought of the birth and beauty of Sri Kṛshṇa, the Āzhwār would fall into a deep trance for months together.

Nammāzhwār is the seer of the Drāviḍa Vedas. He sang four immortal works that are revered as the Tamizh counterparts of the four Vedas.

Nammāzhwār remained on earth in his bodily form for only thirty-five years. His return to Vaikuṇṭham by the archirādi gati, the path of light, is sung by him in the closing portion of the Tiruvāimozhi.

Kaṇṇinuṇ Siruttāmbu

Madhurakavi composed the Kaṇṇinuṇ Siruttāmbu, a short prabandham of only eleven verses in praise of Nammāzhwār, which holds a central place in the tradition. Madhurakavi carried the music of Nammāzhwār's verses far and wide. It is said that in those days everyone, whether boatman, trader, chieftain or brāhmaṇa, attained a transcendent state simply by singing them.

The Four Works of Nammāzhwār

Nammāzhwār gave the essence of the Vedas in Tamizh in the following works.

Tiruviruttam

This holds the essence of the Ṛg Veda. "Tiru" means śrī, sacred. It is a poem of one hundred stanzas of four lines each. Viruttam is a form of poetry, and the word itself means an event; here the event is the soul falling in love with the Supreme Being, told in poetry as bridal mysticism of great sweetness.

Tiruvāsiriyam

This holds the essence of the Yajur Veda. It is a poem of seven sections, seven poems of unequal length, seventy-one lines in all. Its unbroken flow, describing the radiant beauty of the Lord, carries the reader to ethereal heights.

Periya Tiruvandādi

This holds the essence of the Atharvaṇa Veda. It is a poem of eighty-seven lyrical stanzas, simple and direct, moving and inspiring, and it leads the reader to see the Lord face to face.

Tiruvāimozhi

This holds the essence of the Sāma Veda. Its name means "divine words," and it is the magnum opus of Nammāzhwār and the great treasure of Sri Vaishṇavam. It consists of 1,102 Pāsurams of four lines each, arranged in groups of eleven; one group, an exception, has thirteen. Each group is itself called a Tiruvāimozhi, and ten such groups form a pattu, "ten" in Tamizh. The Tiruvāimozhi therefore has ten pattus, one hundred Tiruvāimozhis, and 1,102 Pāsurams. When these Pāsurams are sung together by devotees, their melody is a feast to the ears.
